claim: Regional factors (country and continent) had the largest interaction with gut microbiome composition.
source: Regional factors namely country and continent had the largest interaction with gut microbiome composition (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Age followed by study-condition (disease versus control status) were the second major effect on gut microbiome composition.
source: Age followed by study-condition (disease versus control status) were the second major effect.
evidence: Based on PERMANOVA analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elderly controls had a significantly distinct microbiome composition compared to the young and the middle-aged (p<0.001).
source: PERMANOVA analysis of the gut microbiome composition (after adjusting for country and the DNA extraction technique) indicated that the elderly controls had a significantly distinct microbiome composition compared to the young and the middle-aged (p<0.001) (Figure 1B), in line with our previous findings (Claesson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by PERMANOVA statistical analysis and referenced to previous findings by Claesson et al., 2012.

claim: For three diseases (T2D, CRC and intestinal polyps), the effect of age on gut microbiome was higher than that of the disease itself.
source: Notably, for three diseases (T2D, CRC and intestinal polyps), this effect was higher than that of the disease itself (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on PERMANOVA R2 values comparing age-group and disease status effects shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For three of the diseases (IBD, CRC and Polyps), the effect of the interaction of disease with age-group was significant (all with p<0.05).
source: For three of the diseases (IBD, CRC and Polyps), the effect of the interaction of disease with age-group was significant (all with p<0.05; PERMANOVA after adjusting for the confounders as above).
evidence: Based on PERMANOVA analysis results presented in Table 2.

claim: The effect of interaction between disease and age-group was marginally significant for T2D (p<0.08).
source: The effect was also marginally significant for T2D (p<0.08; PERMANOVA).
evidence: Based on PERMANOVA analysis results.

claim: IBD and CRC had the highest influence of age as a covariate of disease signatures.
source: Further investigation of these influences (measured by the R2) also indicated that, while IBD and CRC had the highest influence of age as a covariate of disease signatures, with T2D and Polyps relatively lower but significant influences (Table 2).
evidence: Based on R-squared values from PERMANOVA analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: In 10 of the 13 disease-age group scenarios (covering five diseases), classifiers trained and tested on the same age-group had significantly higher disease prediction AUC than when tested on different age-groups.
source: Specifically, in 10 of the 13 disease-age group scenarios (covering five diseases), classifiers trained and tested on the same age-group had significantly higher disease prediction AUC than when tested on different age-groups (Figure 2), with the improvement of classification performance significantly higher than would be expected by random chance (obtained using the permutation test based strategy) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on Random Forest classifier analysis results shown in Figure 2 and validated by permutation tests in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CRC and Polyps were characterized by a noticeable decrease in classification AUCs in the elderly age-groups.
source: CRC and Polyps were characterized by noticeably similar age-specific trends wherein the elderly age-groups had a noticeable decrease in classification AUCs (that is lower AUCs for classifiers trained or tested on the elderly age-groups), indicating that the microbiome-disease signatures for these diseases in the elderly age-groups are weaker (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on Random Forest classifier AUC results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The proportion of age-influenced markers ranged from 30% in CRC to 50% in IBD.
source: Comparing the top 85 percentile markers across the different age-groups revealed that the proportion of age-influenced markers (or markers differentially associated across at least one age-group) ranged from 30% in CRC to 50% in IBD (greater than 35% for the other three) (Figure 3—source data 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on analysis of Random Forest feature importance scores across age groups.

claim: 40% of taxa identified in the original study for Polyps displayed significant differences in their feature importance scores across age-groups.
source: Comparing the list of these associations with a pre-compiled list of all known marker associations reported in the original studies (Figure 3—source data 3) (Feng et al., 2015; Franzosa et al., 2019; Karlsson et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2014; Vogtmann et al., 2016; Zeller et al., 2014), identified that 40% of taxa identified in the original study for Polyps, more than 63% for CRC and IBD, 58% for T2D and 25% for Cirrhosis, displayed significant differences in their feature importance scores across age-groups, thereby emphasizing that age-linked disease-microbiome associations are prevalent across diseases (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Based on comparison of Random Forest feature importance scores with previously reported disease markers.

claim: More than 63% of taxa identified in the original studies for CRC and IBD displayed significant differences in their feature importance scores across age-groups.
source: Comparing the list of these associations with a pre-compiled list of all known marker associations reported in the original studies (Figure 3—source data 3) (Feng et al., 2015; Franzosa et al., 2019; Karlsson et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2014; Vogtmann et al., 2016; Zeller et al., 2014), identified that 40% of taxa identified in the original study for Polyps, more than 63% for CRC and IBD, 58% for T2D and 25% for Cirrhosis, displayed significant differences in their feature importance scores across age-groups, thereby emphasizing that age-linked disease-microbiome associations are prevalent across diseases (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Based on comparison of Random Forest feature importance scores with previously reported disease markers.

claim: 58% of taxa identified in the original study for T2D displayed significant differences in their feature importance scores across age-groups.
source: Comparing the list of these associations with a pre-compiled list of all known marker associations reported in the original studies (Figure 3—source data 3) (Feng et al., 2015; Franzosa et al., 2019; Karlsson et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2014; Vogtmann et al., 2016; Zeller et al., 2014), identified that 40% of taxa identified in the original study for Polyps, more than 63% for CRC and IBD, 58% for T2D and 25% for Cirrhosis, displayed significant differences in their feature importance scores across age-groups, thereby emphasizing that age-linked disease-microbiome associations are prevalent across diseases (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Based on comparison of Random Forest feature importance scores with previously reported disease markers.

claim: 25% of taxa identified in the original study for Cirrhosis displayed significant differences in their feature importance scores across age-groups.
source: Comparing the list of these associations with a pre-compiled list of all known marker associations reported in the original studies (Figure 3—source data 3) (Feng et al., 2015; Franzosa et al., 2019; Karlsson et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2014; Vogtmann et al., 2016; Zeller et al., 2014), identified that 40% of taxa identified in the original study for Polyps, more than 63% for CRC and IBD, 58% for T2D and 25% for Cirrhosis, displayed significant differences in their feature importance scores across age-groups, thereby emphasizing that age-linked disease-microbiome associations are prevalent across diseases (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Based on comparison of Random Forest feature importance scores with previously reported disease markers.

claim: From among the refined cross-cohort associated subset of 19 CRC-associated taxa, 13 (67%) had differential association with either of the age-groups (with FDR corrected p-value<0.1) in Training Set 1.
source: From among the refined cross-cohort associated subset of 19 CRC-associated taxa (Thomas et al., 2019), 13 (67%) had differential association with either of the age-groups (with FDR corrected p-value<0.1) in Training Set 1.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of CRC markers across age groups in Training Set 1.

claim: Nine of the 13 CRC-associated taxa with differential age-group associations (77%) could be replicated with the same directionality in Training Set 2.
source: Nine of these (77%) could be replicated with the same directionality in the Training Set 2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on validation analysis across independent CRC cohorts.

claim: Six of the top CRC-predictive features were found to be associated with higher predictive power only in the young/middle age category.
source: Interestingly, from among the top CRC-predictive features reported in the recent meta-analysis, six were found to be associated with higher predictive power only in the young/middle age category (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on analysis of feature importance scores across age groups shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The inter-training-cohort distances obtained for the elderly-specific disease classifiers were significantly higher than those for young/middle-aged individuals (p<2.2e-16).
source: However, in this specific case, while the classifier profiles for the young/middle-aged individuals across the two cohorts were relatively similar, the inter-training-cohort distances obtained for the elderly-specific disease classifiers were significantly higher (indicating variable disease signature and loss of reproducibility) (p<2.2e-16; Mann Whitney Test) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on Mann Whitney Test comparing Spearman distances of feature rank profiles across cohorts.

claim: Five of the top ten CRC markers showed significantly higher prevalence rates in the elderly controls reproducibly across both datasets.
source: Although no specific trends were observed when comparing abundances of the known CRC-specific markers, five of the top ten markers (Fusobacterium nucleatum, Peptostreptococcus stomatis, Gemella morbillorum, Parvimonas micra and Parvimonas spp) showed significantly higher prevalence rates in the elderly controls (reproducibly across both datasets) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of prevalence rates across age groups shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For four of the five diseases (i.e. except polyps), there was a significant change in the directionality of the microbiome alteration, characterized by a significant reduction in the number of gained features with older age (Fishers' exact test p<0.05).
source: For four of the five diseases (i.e. except polyps), there was a significant change in the directionality of the microbiome alteration, characterized by a significant reduction in the number of gained features with older age (Fishers' exact test p<0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Fisher's exact test comparing directionality of taxon associations across age groups.

claim: For elderly, microbiome alterations (for all diseases except cirrhosis and polyps) were characterized by a significant increase in the number of lost taxa.
source: For elderly, microbiome alterations (for all diseases except cirrhosis and polyps) were characterized by a significant increase in the number of lost taxa (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on analysis of directionality of taxon associations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The performances of the generic disease prediction models in the young/middle-aged was high (median AUC: 0.79).
source: While the performances of the generic disease prediction models in the young/middle-aged was high (median AUC: 0.79) and similar to those reported by earlier studies (Pasolli et al., 2016), the same models applied to data from elderly subjects had significantly lower performance AUC (p<1e-7) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on Random Forest classifier AUC results and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Generic disease prediction models applied to data from elderly subjects had significantly lower performance AUC (p<1e-7) compared to young/middle-aged.
source: While the performances of the generic disease prediction models in the young/middle-aged was high (median AUC: 0.79) and similar to those reported by earlier studies (Pasolli et al., 2016), the same models applied to data from elderly subjects had significantly lower performance AUC (p<1e-7) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of Random Forest classifier AUCs across age groups.

claim: In generic disease prediction models, the specificity of prediction (accuracy of identifying healthy individuals) was significantly lower for the elderly.
source: Moreover, in these models, while no significant differences were observed with respect to the disease prediction sensitivities (p<0.13), the specificity of prediction (that is the accuracy of identifying healthy individuals) was significantly lower for the elderly.
evidence: Based on analysis of Random Forest classifier performance metrics.

claim: For both Europe and North America, the gut microbiome from elderly individuals was significantly more variable compared to young and middle-aged controls.
source: In line with our hypothesis, for both Europe and North America, the gut microbiome from elderly individuals was significantly more variable compared to young and middle-aged controls.
evidence: Based on analysis of intra age-group Spearman distances shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increased variability of elderly gut microbiome was not observed in the Asian (Chinese) cohort.
source: However, this was not observed in the Asian (Chinese) cohort.
evidence: Based on analysis of intra age-group Spearman distances shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A total of 61 taxa showed consistent directionality of association with multiple diseases in either young/middle-aged or the elderly age-groups.
source: We identified a total of 61 taxa that showed consistent directionality of association with multiple diseases in either young/middle-aged or the elderly age-groups (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on analysis of taxon associations across multiple diseases shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Streptococcus anginosus and Fusobacterium nucleatum were detected as gained in multiple diseases.
source: For example, Streptococcus anginosus and Fusobacterium nucleatum were detected as gained in multiple diseases.
evidence: Based on analysis of shared disease response markers.

claim: Species belonging to Roseburia spp. (R. hominis) were lost across multiple diseases.
source: Similarly, species belonging to Roseburia spp. (R. hominis) were lost.
evidence: Based on analysis of shared disease response markers.

claim: A group of Clostridia (C. bolteae, C. symbiosum, C. hathewayi, C. citronae, C. asparagiforme) was gained across diseases in both elderly and young/middle aged groups (G1 group).
source: Finally, we identified a distinct group of species (G1) that was gained across diseases in both elderly and young/middle aged groups. These included a group of Clostridia (C. bolteae, C. symbiosum, C. hathewayi, C. citronae, C. asparagiforme) (Figure 5C; see Figure 5—source data 1 for individual diseases).
evidence: Based on analysis of shared disease response markers shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Using Random Forest regression, frailty of an individual could be predicted based on the taxonomic composition of the gut microbiome (R = 0.79).
source: Using Random Forest regression (with five-fold cross validation), we could predict the frailty of an individual (testing both community- and residential care-dwelling subjects) based on the taxonomic composition of the gut microbiome (R = 0.79; Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Random Forest regression analysis results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The G1 group of taxa had the highest mean rank of feature importance scores for frailty (FIM) prediction.
source: Validating our previous observations, the G1 group of taxa had the highest mean rank of feature importance scores for frailty (Functional Independence Measure (FIM)) prediction, indicating that this group had the highest predictive power for frailty in the ELDERMET subjects (Figure 6B), followed by the G2 group (increased across multiple diseases only in the elderly).
evidence: Based on analysis of Random Forest feature importance scores for frailty prediction shown in Figure 6B.

claim: An optimal number of eight taxa had the highest frailty predictive ability.
source: An optimal number of eight taxa had the highest frailty predictive ability (Figure 5C; Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Random Forest regression analysis optimizing number of features.

claim: All eight taxa with highest frailty predictive ability were more abundant with frailty (negatively correlated with FIM and positively associated with Frailty).
source: All these taxa were more abundant with frailty (negatively correlated with FIM and positively associated with Frailty) (Figure 6—source data 1A–B).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis between taxa abundance and frailty measures.

claim: Five of the eight taxa with highest frailty predictive ability belonged to the G1 group.
source: Five of the eight taxa belonged to the G1 group (Figure 6C; Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on comparison of frailty markers with disease-associated taxa groups.

claim: A total of 13 metabolite profiles were significantly associated with the eight frailty-marker taxa.
source: We first focussed on the group of frailty marker taxa and identified 13 metabolic profiles (Figure 6D) that were significantly associated with the eight frailty-marker taxa (See Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on statistical association analysis between taxa and metabolite profiles.

claim: The subset of 13 metabolite profiles alone could predict frailty with a R value of 0.60.
source: This subset of 13 metabolite profiles alone could predict frailty with a R value of 0.60 (between the actual and predicted FIM values), which is significantly higher than that obtained after removing these features from the metabolite profile (Figure 6D; Top panel second from left).
evidence: Based on Random Forest regression analysis using metabolite profiles.

claim: The fecal metabolomes of frail individuals were characterized by significantly higher levels of LCA (along with its derivatives) and DCA (p<0.006).
source: We validated this predicted metabolic functionality against the experimentally measured fecal metabolomic profiles for ELDERMET subjects, where the fecal metabolomes of frail individuals were characterized by significantly higher levels of LCA (along with its derivatives) and DCA (p<0.006) and significantly lower levels of CA and CDCA (p<0.02), as compared to the non-frail individuals (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of measured fecal metabolite levels between frail and non-frail individuals.

claim: The fecal metabolomes of frail individuals were characterized by significantly lower levels of CA and CDCA (p<0.02) compared to non-frail individuals.
source: We validated this predicted metabolic functionality against the experimentally measured fecal metabolomic profiles for ELDERMET subjects, where the fecal metabolomes of frail individuals were characterized by significantly higher levels of LCA (along with its derivatives) and DCA (p<0.006) and significantly lower levels of CA and CDCA (p<0.02), as compared to the non-frail individuals (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of measured fecal metabolite levels between frail and non-frail individuals.

claim: Measured p-cresol negatively correlated with FIM (p<0.01; R = −0.29 with FIM across community and longstay; R = −0.47 for only long-stay).
source: Two other metabolite functionalities associated with the frailty-specific markers that were also validated in the fecal metabolome profile were p-cresol production (measured p-cresol negatively correlated with FIM: p<0.01; R = −0.29 with FIM across community and longstay; R = −0.47 for only long-stay) and ethanol production (significantly higher levels in the fecal metabolome of frail individuals in the long-stay cohort, as compared to the non-frail individuals: p<0.02).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis between measured metabolite levels and FIM scores.

claim: Ethanol levels were significantly higher in the fecal metabolome of frail individuals in the long-stay cohort compared to non-frail individuals (p<0.02).
source: Two other metabolite functionalities associated with the frailty-specific markers that were also validated in the fecal metabolome profile were p-cresol production (measured p-cresol negatively correlated with FIM: p<0.01; R = −0.29 with FIM across community and longstay; R = −0.47 for only long-stay) and ethanol production (significantly higher levels in the fecal metabolome of frail individuals in the long-stay cohort, as compared to the non-frail individuals: p<0.02).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of measured metabolite levels between frail and non-frail individuals.

claim: The abundance of the specific bacterial CutC enzyme was significantly higher in the gut microbiome of the frail individuals.
source: Profiling the abundance (normalized by sequencing depth) of the specific bacterial CutC enzyme catalysing this conversion revealed significantly higher representation in the gut microbiome of the frail individuals (Figure 6D; Upper right panel).
evidence: Based on analysis of humann2 gene family abundance data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Alterations in the gut microbiome have been reported for many diseases.
source: Alterations in the gut microbiome have been reported for many diseases (Duvallet et al., 2017; Pasolli et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous meta-analyses.

claim: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is characterized by an increase (or gain) of pathobionts (such as Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas).
source: While certain diseases like colorectal cancer (CRC) are characterized by an increase (or gain) of pathobionts (such as Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas), the onset of others like Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is associated with the depletion of specific taxa (e.g. Roseburia, Faecalibacterium) (Duvallet et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duvallet et al., 2017 meta-analysis.

claim: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is associated with the depletion of specific taxa (e.g. Roseburia, Faecalibacterium).
source: While certain diseases like colorectal cancer (CRC) are characterized by an increase (or gain) of pathobionts (such as Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas), the onset of others like Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is associated with the depletion of specific taxa (e.g. Roseburia, Faecalibacterium) (Duvallet et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duvallet et al., 2017 meta-analysis.

claim: Diarrhoeal diseases are accompanied by both an increase of pathobionts (specifically Enterobacteriaceae) as well as lower abundance of commensal taxa.
source: In contrast, diarrhoeal diseases are accompanied by both an increase of pathobionts (specifically Enterobacteriaceae) as well as lower abundance of commensal taxa.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Variations in region/ethnicity of subjects are linked to the gut microbiome composition and microbiome-based diagnostics in various diseases.
source: Variations in region/ethnicity of subjects are linked to the gut microbiome composition and microbiome-based diagnostics in various diseases (Deschasaux et al., 2018; He et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Multiple studies have shown age to be a strong covariate of microbiome composition.
source: In addition to region/ethnicity-specific variations, multiple studies have also shown age to be a strong covariate of microbiome composition (Falony et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Falony et al., 2016.

claim: Ageing-associated microbiome alterations in the ELDERMET cohort are associated with lower complexity dietary intake and poly-pharmacy.
source: We, along with others, have previously identified ageing-associated microbiome alterations in the ELDERMET cohort, associated with lower complexity dietary intake and poly-pharmacy (Claesson et al., 2012; O'Toole and Jeffery, 2015; Ticinesi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on the ELDERMET cohort.

claim: Early and late-onset variants of different diseases are characterized by distinct patho-physiologies.
source: Besides ageing-associated changes in the microbiome, early and late-onset variants of different diseases are characterized by distinct patho-physiologies (Duricova et al., 2014; Yeo et al., 2017), which could also be linked to age-related microbiome involvement.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The curated MetagenomicData repository contains taxonomic and functional pathway profiles of more than 6000 shotgun-sequenced human microbiome samples from different human body sites, spanning more than 30 diseases from more than 25 different studies.
source: The curated MetagenomicData repository of the ExperimentHub R library contains taxonomic and functional pathway profiles of more than 6000 shotgun-sequenced human microbiome samples from different human body sites, spanning more than 30 diseases (and controls) from more than 25 different studies (Pasolli et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pasolli et al., 2017 describing the repository.

claim: The curatedMetagenomicData microbiome profiles were created using uniform bioinformatic analysis of the sequenced reads (using metaphlan2 and humann2).
source: A further advantage of the curatedMetagenomicData is that these microbiome profiles were created using uniform bioinformatic analysis of the sequenced reads (using metaphlan2 and humann2) (Franzosa et al., 2018; Truong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to the bioinformatic tools used.

claim: The study analysed the gut microbiome in 15 studies encompassing four diseases, comprising more than 2500 individuals ranging from 20 to 89 years of age.
source: Here we analysed the gut microbiome in 15 studies encompassing four diseases, comprising more than 2500 individuals ranging from 20 to 89 years of age, derived from the ExperimentHub repository, the ELDERMET project and recently published studies on IBD) and colorectal cancer CRC (Franzosa et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2019; Wirbel et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of the study dataset and sources.

claim: Samples from one study (SchirmerC_2016) using a DNA extraction technique tagged as 'Illuminakit' had a distinct taxonomic profile and were removed from analyses.
source: We established that while read lengths had a marginal effect (R = 9e-3, p<0.09) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), samples from one of the studies (SchirmerC_2016) (Schirmer et al., 2016), using a DNA extraction technique tagged as 'Illuminakit' in the metadata, had a distinct taxonomic profile. We removed the 465 samples of this study from all further analyses, thereby reducing the effect of extraction methodology on taxonomic profiles (p<0.06; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Based on envfit analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Half of the eight disease cohorts analyzed featured a significant difference in the age of the control and diseased individuals (i.e. they were not age matched).
source: Among the eight disease cohorts (in the curatedMetagenomicData) that we analyzed here, we discovered that half of these featured a significant difference in the age of the control and diseased individuals (i.e. they were not age matched) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of age distributions shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Clostridium scindens and Clostridium leptum were previously implicated in Clostridium difficile resistance and IBD, respectively.
source: The two species associated with this functionality, namely Clostridium scindens and Clostridium leptum, did not belong to either the G1 or G2 groups of species (contrary to their frailty-association in this study). These species were previously implicated in Clostridium difficile resistance and IBD, respectively (Buffie et al., 2015; Manichanh et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Production of higher levels of hydrophobic bile acids has been associated with the onset of CRC and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).
source: Contrary to their therapeutic relevance, this specific functionality of these species, namely production of higher levels of hydrophobic bile acids, has also been associated with the onset of CRC and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) (Tsuei et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsuei et al., 2014.

claim: A recent meta-analysis of CRC gut microbiomes predicted increased production of secondary bile-acids to be a key CRC-specific functional signature.
source: One of the recent meta-analyses of CRC gut microbiomes also predicted increased production of secondary bile-acids to be a key CRC-specific functional signature (Wirbel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wirbel et al., 2019.

claim: p-cresol is a cytotoxic compound produced by specific gut bacterial species including C. difficile that is associated with microbiome alteration, large bowel cancer and insulin resistance.
source: While p-cresol is a cytotoxic compound (produced by specific gut bacterial species including C. difficile) that is associated with microbiome alteration, large bowel cancer and insulin resistance (Fau et al., 1976; Khan et al., 2014), high level ethanol production in the gut has not only been linked to incidence of NAFLD, atherosclerosis and SIBO, but also to an increase in the levels of inflammatory markers (Elshaghabee et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High level ethanol production in the gut has been linked to incidence of NAFLD, atherosclerosis and SIBO, and to an increase in the levels of inflammatory markers.
source: While p-cresol is a cytotoxic compound (produced by specific gut bacterial species including C. difficile) that is associated with microbiome alteration, large bowel cancer and insulin resistance (Fau et al., 1976; Khan et al., 2014), high level ethanol production in the gut has not only been linked to incidence of NAFLD, atherosclerosis and SIBO, but also to an increase in the levels of inflammatory markers (Elshaghabee et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elshaghabee et al., 2016.

claim: Production of acetone and ammonia (NH3) have been associated with increased cytotoxicity, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, as well as insulin resistance.
source: Similarly, production of acetone, ammonia (NH3) have been associated with increased cytotoxicity, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, as well as insulin resistance (Baskaran et al., 1989; Ghoshal et al., 2017; Khan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Specific gut microbial species including C. citroniae, C. clostridioforme and C. hathewayi degrade choline to trimethylamine, which is linked with atherosclerosis.
source: Another functionality associated with the frailty markers was choline consumption and Trimethylamine (TMA) production. Specific gut microbial species including C. citroniae, C. clostridioforme and C. hathewayi degrade choline to trimethylamine, which is liked with atherosclerosis (Martínez-del Campo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martínez-del Campo et al., 2015.

claim: The association of choline degradation with CRC has been reported in one of the meta-analysis datasets used in the current study.
source: This association with CRC has also been reported in one of the meta-analysis datasets used in the current study (Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2019.

claim: A recent study of the gut microbiome of Thai individuals migrating to the US observed the loss of metabolic functions linked to degradation of dietary fibers with increasing duration of stay.
source: A recent study of the gut microbiome of Thai individuals migrating to the US observed the loss of metabolic functions linked to degradation of dietary fibers like xylan, arabinoxylan, cellobiose, pullulan, glucomannan and resistant starch, with increasing duration of stay leading to a broader loss of microbiome function (Vangay et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vangay et al., 2018.

claim: Accounting for age in disease-microbiome classifiers can potentially inform the development of microbiome-based diagnostic strategies customized for specific age-groups.
source: By identifying specific age-linked microbiome associations for different diseases, this study can potentially inform the development of microbiome-based diagnostic strategies customized for specific age-groups.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study findings.

claim: Microbiome restoration strategies may be more crucial for disease amelioration in elderly subjects as opposed to antibiotic-based eradication regimens.
source: Furthermore, distinct changes observed in the overall directionality of taxon associations (e.g. the gradual shifting to a loss-of-taxa phenotype in the elderly) highlight that microbiome restoration strategies may be more crucial for disease amelioration in elderly subjects (as opposed to antibiotic-based eradication regimens).
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed patterns of taxon loss in elderly.

claim: Specific changes are observed with ageing that can potentially make the host more susceptible to certain microbiome-related diseases.
source: This is especially important since specific changes are observed with ageing that can potentially make the host more susceptible to certain microbiome-related diseases.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study findings on age-related microbiome changes.

claim: With increasing age, a decrease of the core microbiome accompanied by an increase of pathobionts was observed in an earlier study.
source: Interestingly, these findings resonate with the results of one of our earlier studies, where with increasing age, a decrease of the core microbiome accompanied by an increase of pathobionts was observed (O'Toole and Jeffery).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by O'Toole and Jeffery.

claim: The acquisition of a specific subset of disease-associated taxa (G1 group) can shift the metabolic state to a disease-like state.
source: Finally, reproducible identification of a specific set of species markers associated with multiple diseases and their specific metabolite profile (sugar consumption and the production of a range of metabolites that are detrimental for the host) indicates that the acquisition of this subset of disease-associated taxa can shift the metabolic state to a disease-like state.
evidence: Inference drawn from the metabolite profiling and disease association analysis.

claim: Ageing-associated microbiome alterations towards a disease-like configuration occur in colorectal cancer patients, thereby masking disease signatures.
source: Ageing-associated microbiome alterations towards a disease-like configuration occur in colorectal cancer patients, thereby masking disease signatures.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: A microbiome disease response shared across multiple diseases in elderly subjects is distinct from that in young/middle-aged individuals.
source: We identified a microbiome disease response shared across multiple diseases in elderly subjects that is distinct from that in young/middle-aged individuals, but also a novel set of taxa consistently gained in disease across all age groups.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: A novel set of taxa is consistently gained in disease across all age groups.

claim: A subset of taxa consistently gained in disease across all age groups was associated with increased frailty in subjects from the ELDERMET cohort.
source: A subset of these taxa was associated with increased frailty in subjects from the ELDERMET cohort.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: The relevant taxa differentially encode specific functions that are known to have disease associations.
source: The relevant taxa differentially encode specific functions that are known to have disease associations.

claim: The onset of frailty is associated with an increase of SCFA consumption by gut-bacteria accompanied by a concomitant decrease of the production of the SCFA butyrate.
source: Specifically, the onset of frailty is observed to be associated with an increase of SCFA consumption by gut-bacteria (accompanied by a concomitant decrease of the production of the SCFA butyrate), increased consumption of the beneficial amino acid Tryptophan as well as the increased production of the T2D-linked branched chain amino acid Threonine.
evidence: Based on metabolite profile association analysis with frailty.

claim: The onset of frailty is associated with increased consumption of the beneficial amino acid Tryptophan.

evidence: Based on metabolite profile association analysis with frailty.

claim: The abundance of specific microbial pathways for propane-1,2-diol to acetone conversion was predicted to be significantly higher in the microbiome of the frail individuals.
source: Although fecal metabolome data was not available for ExperimentHub microbiome samples, the abundance of specific microbial pathways (obtained using humann2) was associated with the production of these metabolites, namely propane-1,2-diol to acetone, and allantoin to Ammonia/CO2/Glyoxylate was predicted to be significantly higher in the microbiome of the frail individuals (Figure 6D; Lower panel).
evidence: Based on humann2 pathway abundance analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The abundance of specific microbial pathways for allantoin to Ammonia/CO2/Glyoxylate conversion was predicted to be significantly higher in the microbiome of the frail individuals.

claim: The 'gained' groups (G1-G3) were disproportionately associated with the consumption of simple sugars (lactose, psicose, xylose, sucrose, raffinose).
source: Similarly, comparing the metabolic signatures of the taxa in the G1-G3 groups with those of the different groups of lost taxa L1-L3, also revealed an interesting pattern whereby the 'gained' groups were disproportionately associated with the consumption of simple sugars (lactose, psicose, xylose, sucrose, raffinose).
evidence: Based on metabolite profile analysis comparing gained and lost taxa groups.

claim: The 'lost' groups (L1-L3) were enriched for consumption of dietary prebiotics like xylo-oligosaccharides, fructo-oligosaccharides, inulin and production of butyrate and succinate.
source: The 'lost' groups in contrast were enriched for consumption of dietary prebiotics like xylo-oligosaccharides, fructo-oligosaccharides, inulin and production of butyrate and succinate.
evidence: Based on metabolite profile analysis comparing gained and lost taxa groups.

claim: Each of the top frailty-associated markers were identified in the top 15 predictors of frailty independently in individuals with high or low medication.
source: Each of the top frailty-associated markers were not only observed to have significant associations with the different frailty measures even after taking into account for the effect of the selected sets of medication type, but also identified in the top 15 predictors of frailty, independently in the individuals with high or low medication (Figure 5—source data 1c).
evidence: Based on analysis adjusting for medication effects.

claim: A recent study identified cancer stage-microbiome interactions.
source: For example, a recent study identified cancer stage-microbiome interactions (Yachida et al., 2019); however, we also note from the published data that 51% of the younger subjects (less than 60 years of age) presented with Stage III/IV cancer, whereas a significantly higher percentage (71%) of older subjects presented with Stage I/II cancer (p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yachida et al., 2019 and statistical analysis of their data.
